sections.h2: What is Peach County, Georgia, like for someone selling a house?
sections.html:
Peach County is a small central Georgia county with Fort Valley as its seat and Byron as the second city. Its own website describes a place about 90 minutes south of Atlanta where big industry, small business and agriculture meet. Census QuickFacts puts July 2025 population at 29,877, up 6.7 percent from the 2020 estimates base, spread over 150.28 square miles of land at 186.2 people per square mile.

Homes here cost far less than in the Atlanta suburbs. The median owner-occupied home was worth $207,800 for 2020 to 2024, and 69.6 percent of homes are owner-occupied, the lowest owner share of the four Georgia counties in the same comparison. Median gross rent was $940 and the median household income was $71,293. The county recorded 139 building permits in 2025, and 18.8 percent of residents are 65 or older.

That mix of renters, older owners and modest values shapes the tax questions sellers ask. Many Peach County sellers have inherited a house, rented one out, or fallen behind on a bill. The tax offices described below can give a payoff figure for any of those cases.

sections.h2: Where do I go for Peach County property tax questions?
sections.html:
The Tax Commissioner bills and collects. The Board of Tax Assessors values property, takes exemption applications and handles appeals. Peach County's own assessor pages say the commissioner has no role in appraisal or in setting the millage rate, and that the county commissioners only appoint and fund the assessors.

The commissioner's office keeps Monday to Friday hours from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Its site covers county tax only. The city tax page lists separate district codes for Byron, Fort Valley, Perry and Warner Robins, a reminder that parts of this county's tax base fall inside several city limits. Ask the city finance office what a city bill looks like if your house sits inside one of them.

sections.h2: When is Peach County property tax due?
sections.html:
The commissioner's FAQ says real estate and business personal property taxes are normally due by December 20. Mobile and modular homes are due April 1, and motor vehicle tax follows the primary owner's birthday. Because the date can change from year to year, read the due date printed on your bill.

Late charges on real estate follow a simple schedule:

  • Interest of 1 percent per month is charged after the due date.
  • A 10 percent penalty applies to taxes not paid within 90 days of the deadline.
  • Homesteaded property with a tax liability under $500 is spared the 90-day penalty.
  • If the bill stays unpaid, the commissioner has the right and the duty to levy on the property.

The commissioner's home page has announced delinquent tax sales at the Peach County Courthouse at 205 W Church Street in Fort Valley, including one scheduled for March 3, 2026 at 10 a.m. The office posts a tax sale list for download. If your parcel could appear on a list like that, ask the commissioner for a payoff before you list the house.

sections.h2: How does a Peach County assessment appeal work?
sections.html:
You have 45 days from the date of the assessment notice to appeal to the Board of Equalization or to an arbitrator. After that decision you may continue to Superior Court by sending the Board of Tax Assessors a written notice. The assessors' page cites O.C.G.A. 48-5-311 as the authority for the appeal.

Keep these points in mind when you decide whether an appeal is worth the effort:

  • Georgia assesses property at 40 percent of fair market value unless a statute says otherwise (O.C.G.A. 48-5-7).
  • The notice and the tax bill both show the fair market value and the assessed value.
  • Fair market value means what a knowledgeable buyer would pay and a willing seller would accept in an arm's length sale.
  • Peach County says its assessors review property annually and may enter a parcel during business hours, with identification, to check data after a permit, a sale or an appeal.

Think about how a recent contract price compares with the notice before you contest a value on a house you plan to sell.

sections.h2: Which homestead exemptions apply in Peach County?
sections.html:
A homeowner who owns and occupies the house as a permanent residence on January 1 can claim the standard exemption, which the county lists as $2,000 off the 40 percent assessed value for state, county and school taxes. Applications are made with the Tax Assessor's Office, and the county says the window runs from April 2 of the prior year through April 1 of the year the exemption is first sought.

The county's exemption page lists these programs:

  • $4,000 for owners 65 or older, if income for the owner and spouse does not exceed $10,000 for the prior year (retirement, pension and disability income is excluded up to the Social Security maximum).
  • An added school-tax exemption of up to $10,000 of assessed value for owners 62 or older under the same income test.
  • A floating exemption for owners 62 or older with household income of $30,000 or less, which the county warns can actually raise a bill.
  • Disabled veteran and surviving spouse exemptions, which the page lists at $109,986 for the 2023 tax year.

Bring proof of age, a warranty deed and income statements as the facts require. Refinancing or any deed change means a new application, and a buyer must file for the exemption on the new home. Freeport exemptions for manufacturing and warehouse inventory are filed with the assessors by April 1.

sections.h2: How should a seller handle Peach County property tax at closing?
sections.html:
Start with a payoff request to the tax commissioner at 478-825-3161, so you know whether current taxes, interest or a prior-year balance sits on the parcel. Have the closing attorney build the proration into the settlement statement, because the sale contract decides how the year's tax is divided.

If the buyer pays off a bill that includes city tax, remember that Fort Valley and Byron levy their own. Ask the commissioner whether the parcel is billed through the county alone or has a city component. Mobile homes are billed separately and are due April 1, so a manufactured home on the lot may carry its own balance.

The buyer needs to file a new homestead application after closing. The seller should tell the assessors when the exemption no longer applies, since the county asks owners to report any loss of eligibility.

faqs.q: When are Peach County real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: The commissioner's FAQ says December 20 is the normal date for real estate and business personal property. Mobile homes are due April 1, so confirm the exact date on your bill.

faqs.q: What is the late penalty in Peach County?
faqs.a: Interest of 1 percent a month applies after the due date, and a 10 percent penalty applies after 90 days. Homestead property owing under $500 does not get the 90-day penalty.

faqs.q: How do I appeal a Peach County property value?
faqs.a: File within 45 days of the assessment notice date, with the Board of Equalization or an arbitrator. A later step to Superior Court needs a written notice to the Board of Tax Assessors.

faqs.q: Where do I apply for a homestead exemption in Peach County?
faqs.a: Apply at the Tax Assessor's Office in Fort Valley, with a warranty deed and any proof the exemption requires. The deadline to receive the benefit for the same year is April 1.

faqs.q: Does Peach County tax mobile homes?
faqs.a: Yes. Mobile and modular homes are taxed as personal property, due April 1, and the current year's tax must be paid in full before a location permit is issued.
